title: The Angelus
hookLine: the noon bell, three verses, three Hail Marys, remembering the angel came

cards: There's a French painting from the 1850s. Two peasants, a man and a woman, stand in a flat, brown field at the end of the day. A pitchfork is stuck in the ground.
A basket of potatoes sits at their feet. Far off on the horizon, there's a tiny church steeple. The man has taken off his hat.
The woman's hands are folded and her head is bowed. They've stopped working, in the middle of the field, because the church bell has just rung.
The painter, Jean-François Millet, named the painting after the prayer they're saying.

teach.h: THE ANGEL OF THE LORD DECLARED.
teach.b: The Angelus takes its name from its first words in Latin: Angelus Domini nuntiavit Mariae. The angel of the Lord declared unto Mary.
Traditionally, church bells rang it three times a day, morning, noon and evening, in a pattern of three strokes, a pause, three, a pause, three, then nine.

The custom was to stop wherever you were: in the field, the kitchen, the market. The prayer walks through the moment the angel Gabriel came to Mary, in three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary.
First: the angel declared unto Mary, and she conceived of the Holy Spirit.

Second, Mary's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Third, from the opening of John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

At that line, people traditionally kneel or bow. Then a short closing prayer. Catholics believe that in that moment God took on a human body: the eternal Word came into time and flesh and a small town.
So three times a day, in the middle of ordinary work, the Angelus remembers that God came into ordinary life.

teach.h: AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH, AND DWELT AMONG US.
teach.b: In the Easter season the Regina Caeli takes its place: Queen of Heaven, rejoice. And every Sunday at noon, the Pope still leads the Angelus from a window over Saint Peter's Square.
That closes this part of the camp, the body praying: walking in the door, holy water, the bended knee, the Glory Be, the Creed, the morning offering, and now a bell at noon.

how: Catholics traditionally pray the Angelus at 6 a.m., noon and 6 p.m., often at the ringing of a church bell: three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary, and a closing prayer; in the Easter season the Regina Caeli is prayed instead, and the Pope leads it from his window every Sunday at noon.

games.why: that's the scene Millet painted: a man with his hat off, a woman with folded hands, praying the Angelus right there in the field.

practice: Picture noon wherever you'll be, at a desk, in a car, in line, and picture stopping there for thirty seconds, the way the two peasants stopped in the field.
If you pray, say one Hail Mary; it begins, in the Douay-Rheims, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." If you don't, look up from the work, and let the middle of the day be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Angelus. Latin for angel: a prayer at morning, noon and evening, remembering the angel came to Mary, and the Word was made flesh.

orig.note: Latin: the angel of the Lord declared unto Mary, the first words that give the prayer its name.

carryVoice: Your line: the word was made flesh. Three bells a day remember it. Go gently.
